newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Up to 40 believed killed in wake of Cambodia coup.
newsitem.headline: Up to 40 believed killed in wake of Cambodia coup.

text.p: Up to 40 Cambodians have been killed since the overthrow of the first prime minister but it was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge, a diplomatic source said on Wednesday.

The source, who declined to be identified, said there was evidence of torture among some of the victims, including four bodyguards of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay.
The guards were found dead with their eyes gouged out.
"It's very unclear if this is a centrally orchestrated, carefully planned purge or more dispersed -- a general uncoordinated attack on FUNCINPEC officials," he said.
"But even if it is the latter, it could be stopped," he said.

"Of course we are afraid. People are being arrested and some have been killed," a youth leader of the royalist FUNCINPEC party told Reuters as he and four other opposition activists were holed up in a small "safe house" in the capital.

The men are uncertain if their lives are actively at risk and Western rights workers with whom they have consulted have no clear idea either. Many other activists like them are also in hiding in Cambodia or have fled the country.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 after a weekend of fighting in the capital.
On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Ung Huot said he was willing to accept the job as Hun Sen's new coalition partner.

Hun Sen has said he wants to preserve the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party. But the only way to maintain the coalition was for FUNCINPEC to choose a new first prime minister to replace Ranariddh.
Ung Huot, a senior FUNCINPEC member, said he would keep his job as foreign minister. He also said he still respected Ranariddh but put the interests of the country first.
"I accept to be first prime minister because I put the interests of my people and my country above everything else," Ung Huot told reporters.
"The interests of the country dictate that Cambodia must go on...We cannot wait," he said. "We've suffered too much."
Hun Sen's CPP accepted Ung Huot's nomination and would support his bid to become first prime minister when it comes up in the National Assembly later this month, an adviser to Hun said.
King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, on Tuesday said he was upset by reports that Hun Sen's police and army had tortured and put to death political opponents and urged an end to the bloodshed.

"I am profoundly distressed at the reports that the military and members of the national police have cruelly tortured and killed without mercy their enemies after having arrested or captured them," Sihanouk said in a letter sent from Beijing to Chea Sim, the acting head of state, in Phnom Penh.
Sihanouk was in Beijing for medical treatment at the time of the coup. Ranariddh left Cambodia days before the coup.
Hundreds of supporters and soldiers loyal to Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party are believed to remain in detention.
Military officials have denied detainees were being mistreated and said they were undergoing "re-education".

Hun Sen said on Tuesday Cambodia would have a free and fair election on May 23 as planned but the United States said that Hun Sen's rhetoric in recent days, seemingly in favour of democracy, was not matched by action.

"(Hun Sen's) words are beautiful over the past 48 hours ... but whether or not he can match those words in reality with his actions is a very big test for him," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing on Tuesday.

Ranariddh, who left the country the day before Hun Sen's forces moved against the prince's troops in the capital, has called for resistance to Hun Sen and appealed to the international community for support.

The prince has pleaded his case in meetings with French and Japanese envoys, the U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and U.S. State Department officials and members of Congress in Washington, but he has received no firm offers of support.

Sam Rainsy, a long-time foe of Hun Sen and an ally of Ranariddh's, was briefly detained by Thai authorities on the border with Cambodia on Wednesday as he tried to enter the western Cambodian town of Poipet.
He came to the border on Tuesday to rally his supporters and organise resistance to Hun Sen.

Hun Sen has denied he staged a coup and justified his forces' move against Ranariddh's men in the capital by saying Ranariddh's military commanders were smuggling defectors from the Maoist Khmer Rouge into the city to bolster the prince's troops strength.
Ranariddh denied he was doing so.
